title: Guidance and Safe Care
bigQuestion: What does it take to keep a child safe and guide their behavior for an evening, a week or a childhood?

story.title: The List on the Fridge
story.kicker: Dani's first paid babysitting job started with a sheet of paper under a magnet, and by nine o'clock she had used every line of it.
paragraphs: Dani was sixteen and had been asked to watch the Okafor kids, Zuri, who was four, and baby Kofi, who was seven months, from six to ten on a Friday. She had her Red Cross babysitting card and a bag with a coloring book, a deck of cards and her phone charger. Mrs. Okafor met her at the door already holding her keys, and walked her straight to the refrigerator.

Under a magnet was a single sheet. Their cell numbers. The pediatrician's number. Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, written in red. The address of the house, because, Mrs. Okafor said, "if you ever have to call 911 you will not remember it." Zuri: allergic to peanuts, EpiPen in the top kitchen drawer, here is how it works, watch me. Kofi: bottle at seven, six ounces, then bed at seven-thirty, on his back, in the crib, nothing in it, sleep sack only. Zuri: bath optional, teeth, two books, lights out at eight, she will ask for a third book, the answer is no. Dani read it twice.

The evening went the way evenings with a four-year-old go. Zuri did not want the chicken; Dani gave her the choice of eating it with ketchup or with the rice mixed in, and she ate it with ketchup. Zuri wanted to climb the bookshelf; Dani did not say "no" thirty times, she got out the couch cushions and made a fort, and the bookshelf was forgotten. Kofi took his bottle, went into his sleep sack, and Dani laid him on his back and stood there a moment, checking the crib the way the card had taught her: firm mattress, fitted sheet, nothing else.

At eight-forty, with Zuri asleep, Dani heard a small sound and found Kofi awake and coughing, red-faced, and for one long second she could not tell whether he was choking or just crying. Then he drew a full breath and howled, and she picked him up and walked him and he settled. Her hands shook. She had known exactly what to do for an infant who could not breathe, five back blows, five chest thrusts, call 911, and she had been ready to do it. She was very glad she had not needed to.

When the Okafors came home Dani told them everything, including the cough, in order, the way the list had been written. Mrs. Okafor said the thing that made Dani a regular for two years: "You didn't just follow the list. You knew why every line was there." This chapter is that list, and the reasons.
story.think: Every line on the refrigerator list was there for a reason. Pick two lines and explain what could go wrong on an ordinary Friday night if that line were missing.

lessons.title: Guidance, Not Punishment
lessons.mainIdea: Guidance teaches a child what to do; punishment only teaches what to avoid when an adult is watching, and hitting a child teaches that hitting works.
reading: A three-year-old throws a cup of milk on the floor. One adult yells, grabs her arm and puts her in a chair facing the wall for ten minutes. Another adult says, "Milk stays in the cup. Here's a towel; let's wipe it up," and hands her the towel. Both adults want the same thing: no more milk on the floor. Only the second one is teaching it. *Guidance* is everything an adult does to help a child learn how to behave. *Punishment* is making a child suffer for what she already did. The first builds a skill. The second builds fear, and fear stops working the moment the adult leaves the room.

The case against spanking is not about being soft. Decades of research have found that children who are hit are more aggressive, not less, and are no better behaved over time. Hitting teaches, very clearly, that a bigger person may hit a smaller one when angry. It also damages the trust that makes every other kind of guidance possible. Yelling and shaming do a milder version of the same harm. And shaking a baby, ever, for any reason, can cause permanent brain injury or death. A crying baby who cannot be soothed goes in the crib on his back, safe, while the adult steps out to breathe.

Guidance starts with expectations that match the age. A one-year-old cannot remember a rule from yesterday. A two-year-old cannot share. A three-year-old cannot sit still for a forty-minute dinner. A four-year-old cannot always tell wishes from facts. Most "misbehavior" in young children is a child doing exactly what a child that age does, in a situation that was set up for an adult. Half of guidance is changing the setup: the fragile thing goes on a high shelf, dinner is twenty minutes, the walk to the car starts with a two-minute warning.

The other half is a small set of tools, taught in the next two lessons: routines, choices, redirection, and natural and logical consequences. Behind all of them is one attitude. The adult is calm, the adult is kind, and the adult means it. A limit stated once in a quiet voice and kept every time is worth more than a threat shouted ten times. Children test limits to find out if they are real. The answer should be boring: yes, every time.

words.d: everything an adult does to help a child learn how to behave, from setting up the room to stating limits calmly
making a child suffer for a past action; it builds fear and avoidance rather than skill
a clear rule about what is allowed, stated calmly and kept the same every time
permanent brain injury or death caused by shaking an infant; never shake a baby for any reason

look.title: The Milk on the Floor, Two Ways
look.text: Adult A: yells "What is wrong with you!", puts the three-year-old in a chair facing the wall, and cleans up the milk himself while she cries. Adult B: says "Milk stays in the cup," hands her a towel, wipes up alongside her, then pours a smaller amount into a cup with a lid. The next night, the child at house A throws the milk again when the adult turns his back. The child at house B carries her lidded cup to the table.
look.prompt: Name three specific things Adult B did that Adult A did not, and explain what the child in each house learned about milk and about the adult.

check.q: What is the main difference between guidance and punishment?
choices: Guidance teaches what to do; punishment makes the child suffer for what was already done
Guidance is for older children and punishment is for toddlers
Guidance is soft and punishment gets results
There is no real difference; both stop the behavior
check.why: Guidance builds a skill the child can use next time. Punishment builds fear that works only while the adult watches.

check.q: Research on spanking has found that children who are hit tend to be:
choices: Better behaved within a few weeks
More aggressive, with no improvement in behavior over time
More attached to the parent who spanks
Unaffected as long as it is done calmly
check.why: Studies consistently link physical punishment to more aggression and no better behavior, and it damages the trust that guidance depends on.

check.q: A babysitter is alone with a two-month-old who has cried for forty minutes and cannot be soothed. She feels her frustration rising. What should she do?
choices: Bounce the baby harder and faster until he stops
Put him face down so the crying is muffled
Put him on his back in the crib, step out of the room to calm down for a few minutes, then check on him and call the parents
Give him a bottle of water to quiet him
check.why: A baby in a safe crib on his back is safe while the adult calms down. Shaking an infant, even briefly, can cause permanent injury.

lessons.title: Routines and Choices
lessons.mainIdea: A predictable routine prevents most battles, and a choice between two acceptable options gives a child real power inside the adult's limit.
reading: Bedtime at the Okafor house goes: bath, pajamas, teeth, two books, song, lights out. Every night. In that order. By the time Zuri was three she could recite it, and mostly she did not fight it, because there was nothing to fight. It was simply what happened after dinner. This is a *routine*: a fixed order of events that happens the same way every time. Routines work because young children cannot tell time and cannot plan, so an unpredictable day feels like a series of ambushes. A predictable day lets the child know what is coming and get ready for it.

Build routines around the hard parts of the day: waking up, leaving the house, meals, naps, cleanup and bedtime. Keep the order the same even when the times shift. Use *transitions*, warnings that a change is coming: "two more turns on the slide, then shoes." Toddlers and preschoolers hate being interrupted mid-thought as much as adults do; a warning lets them finish. A picture chart of the bedtime steps on the wall lets a preschooler run the routine herself, which she will proudly do. School-age children can help write the routine, and children who help write a rule follow it far more often.

Inside a routine, give *choices*. The rule is two options, both of which the adult can live with. "Red cup or blue cup?" "Walk to the car or hop to the car?" "Bath before books or after?" What the choice does is hand the child a small piece of real power at the exact moment she was about to grab for it by saying no. What it must not be is fake. "Do you want to go to bed now?" is not a choice, because the honest answer is no and the adult will not accept it. And "Which do you want, the couch, the chair, the floor, the rug, or my lap?" is too many; a three-year-old freezes.

The principle: most conflict with young children is about control, and a routine plus a choice gives the child control over the things that do not matter so the adult can keep control over the things that do. When Zuri asks for a third book, the answer is no, calmly, the same way every night. Because everything else about bedtime is hers, the no is easy to take.

words.d: a fixed order of daily events that happens the same way every time, so the child knows what is coming
the change from one activity to the next; a warning before it prevents most protests
in guidance, two acceptable options offered to the child so the child has real power inside the adult's limit

look.title: Getting Out the Door
look.text: Every morning is the same fight. Dad says "time to go" while the four-year-old is mid-tower with the blocks. She screams. He carries her to the car without shoes. Coat, shoes and backpack are in three different rooms. Some mornings breakfast happens, some mornings it does not. Dad is late to work three days a week.
look.prompt: Design a morning routine for this family in five steps, in order, and add one transition warning and one two-option choice. Explain which fight each step removes.

check.q: Which of these is a real choice for a three-year-old?
choices: "Do you want to put your pajamas on?"
"Do you want to go to bed or stay up?"
"Pick any pajamas from the whole drawer."
"The dinosaur pajamas or the star pajamas?"
check.why: A real choice offers two options the adult can accept. A yes-or-no question invites no, and an open drawer is too many choices.

check.q: A preschooler screams every time she is told playtime is over. What is the most useful change?
choices: Give a warning a few minutes before the change: "two more turns, then cleanup"
End playtime earlier so she has less to lose
Stop announcing the end and just take the toys away
Let her play until she chooses to stop
check.why: Transition warnings let a child finish a thought and get ready. Most protests at a change are about being interrupted without notice.

check.q: Why does a fixed bedtime routine reduce arguments?
choices: Because it makes the child too tired to argue
Because young children cannot plan or tell time, so a predictable order removes the surprise that causes the protest
Because it lets the adult skip the steps the child dislikes
Because children only argue about new rules, and a routine is never new
check.why: A young child cannot see the day ahead. A routine tells her what comes next, so a change stops feeling like an ambush.

lessons.title: Redirection and Consequences
lessons.mainIdea: Redirect a young child toward what is allowed, and let older children learn from consequences that follow naturally or logically from what they did.
reading: A fourteen-month-old is pulling books off the shelf and chewing on the covers. Saying "no" gets a look and then more chewing, because to a fourteen-month-old "no" is a sound, not a plan. *Redirection* is the tool: take the book gently, hand him a teething ring or a board book that is his to chew, and move him three feet away. "Books are for reading. This one is for chewing." Redirection works for infants and toddlers because it replaces the forbidden thing with an allowed one instead of leaving a hole where the fun was. It works best when the replacement is close by and at least as interesting.

For preschoolers and older, add *natural consequences*: what happens by itself when a child makes a choice, with no adult adding anything. She refuses her coat; she is cold on the walk. He leaves his truck in the driveway; it gets run over. She does not eat dinner; she is hungry before bed and gets the same dinner back, not dessert. The adult's job is to let it happen and skip the lecture. "You're cold. Here's your coat," teaches more than five minutes of "I told you so." Natural consequences are not for danger. A child does not learn about the street by being hit by a car; the adult holds the hand.

When there is no safe natural consequence, use a *logical consequence*: something the adult sets up that is related to the behavior, respectful, and reasonable in size. Crayon on the wall means you help wash the wall. Throwing sand means you leave the sandbox for the rest of the visit. Riding the bike into the street means the bike is put away until tomorrow. The link is what makes it teaching instead of punishment. Losing screen time for a week because of crayon on the wall is unrelated and too big; a four-year-old cannot connect them, so she learns only that the adult is unpredictable.

Two more tools. Ignore what is only annoying: whining, a tantrum in a safe place, a rude word said for effect. Attention feeds behavior, and behavior that gets nothing tends to fade. And catch the child being good, specifically: "You put the cups on the table without being asked." Children repeat what gets noticed. An adult who notices five good things for every limit she sets will find she has to set far fewer limits.

words.d: moving a young child from something not allowed to something that is, by replacing the activity rather than just forbidding it
what happens by itself as a result of a child's choice, with nothing added by the adult; never used where there is danger
a result the adult sets up that is related to the behavior, respectful and reasonable in size

look.title: Match the Tool to the Child
look.text: Situation 1: a 12-month-old keeps grabbing the cat's tail. Situation 2: a 5-year-old refuses to wear a jacket to the park on a cool day. Situation 3: a 7-year-old drew on the hallway wall with marker. Situation 4: a 3-year-old whines "I want juice" in a singsong voice for the fourth time after being told water is what there is. Situation 5: a 4-year-old runs toward the parking lot.
look.prompt: For each situation choose redirection, natural consequence, logical consequence, ignoring, or none of these because it is a safety matter. Say what you would do and why that tool fits the age.

check.q: A six-year-old leaves his bike in the driveway after being reminded, and it gets scratched when the car backs out. What is the best response?
choices: Ground him from all screens for a week
Buy him a new bike so he is not upset
The scratch is the natural consequence; say so briefly, without a lecture, and skip any added punishment
Yell so he remembers next time
check.why: A natural consequence teaches by itself. Adding an unrelated punishment or a lecture weakens the lesson.

check.q: Which consequence is logical for a preschooler who threw sand at another child?
choices: No dessert tonight
No television for the weekend
A ten-minute time-out in the car
Leaving the sandbox for the rest of the visit
check.why: A logical consequence is related to the behavior, respectful and reasonable in size. Leaving the sandbox connects directly to throwing sand.

check.q: A 13-month-old keeps pulling the cat's tail. Which tool fits this age best?
choices: Redirect: move him away and hand him a stuffed animal to pull, saying "gentle"
Explain that the cat has feelings and could be hurt
A time-out chair for one minute
Let the cat scratch him so he learns naturally
check.why: A one-year-old cannot follow an explanation or a time-out. Redirection replaces the activity, and a natural consequence is never used where there is a risk of injury.

lessons.title: Safe Sleep
lessons.mainIdea: Every sleep, every time: on the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the sleep space with nothing else in it.
reading: It is 7:30 p.m. Kofi has finished his bottle and his eyes are closing. Dani carries him to the crib. What she sees should be this: a firm mattress that does not sink under his weight, a fitted sheet pulled tight, and nothing else. No blanket, no pillow, no stuffed animal, no bumper pads around the rails. She lays him down on his *back*, not his side, not his stomach, zipped into a wearable blanket called a sleep sack, and she leaves. That is *safe sleep*, and it is the same every nap and every night until he is one year old.

The reason is *SIDS*, sudden infant death syndrome, and suffocation. In the early 1990s, doctors found that babies put to sleep on their stomachs died in their sleep far more often than babies on their backs. The "Back to Sleep" campaign that followed cut those deaths roughly in half. Soft bedding is the other killer: a baby who rolls face-first into a pillow or a blanket cannot lift her head away. The crib looks bare to an adult. To a baby it is the safest place in the house.

The rest of the rules, from the American Academy of Pediatrics: room-share, not bed-share. The crib or bassinet goes in the parents' room for at least the first six months, but the baby never sleeps in an adult bed, on a couch or in an armchair with an adult; a sleeping adult can roll onto or against a baby. Keep the room a comfortable temperature and do not overdress; a baby who is sweating is too hot. No smoking in the home. Offer a pacifier at sleep time once breastfeeding is settled. Car seats, swings and bouncers are for travel and play, not for sleep; move a baby who falls asleep in one to a flat surface.

A baby who can roll over on his own may end up on his stomach, and that is all right; you still put him down on his back. Grandparents and older relatives often learned different rules, stomach sleeping, a blanket, a bumper to keep arms from getting stuck. The rules changed because babies died. The babysitter's job is to follow the current rule every time, and a parent's job is to tell every caregiver the rule and check that they follow it.

words.d: an infant on the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the sleep space, with nothing else in it, every sleep
sudden infant death syndrome, the unexplained death of a baby under one year during sleep; back sleeping greatly lowers the risk
the baby sleeps in the parents' room in a separate crib or bassinet, not in the adult bed
a wearable blanket that zips around a baby so no loose blanket is needed in the crib

look.title: Inspect the Crib
look.text: You are about to put a five-month-old down for the night. In the crib: a firm mattress with a fitted sheet, a folded quilt at the foot "in case she gets cold," a small stuffed rabbit she likes, and padded bumpers tied to the rails "so she doesn't bump her head." The baby is in a onesie and a sleep sack. The room is warm. Her father says she sleeps better on her tummy.
look.prompt: List every item that comes out of the crib and every instruction you would not follow, and give the reason for each. What stays?

check.q: Which crib is set up for safe sleep?
choices: Firm mattress, fitted sheet, light blanket tucked at the sides
Firm mattress, fitted sheet, nothing else, baby on her back in a sleep sack
Soft mattress topper for comfort, fitted sheet, baby on her side
Firm mattress, bumper pads, one small stuffed toy, baby on her back
check.why: Safe sleep is a bare crib: firm flat surface, fitted sheet, no blankets, bumpers, pillows or toys, and the baby on her back.

check.q: A tired parent falls asleep on the couch holding the baby. Why is this dangerous?
choices: The baby will learn to need being held to sleep
The couch is too cold
A sleeping adult can roll onto the baby, or the baby can slip into a gap and suffocate
Couches are only dangerous for toddlers, not infants
check.why: Adult beds, couches and armchairs are the sleep surfaces where infants are most often suffocated. Room-share, never bed-share or couch-share.

check.q: A seven-month-old is put down on his back and rolls onto his stomach on his own. What should the caregiver do?
choices: Roll him back every time and stay in the room to keep doing it
Prop him on his side with a rolled towel so he cannot roll
Put him in a swing where he cannot roll
Leave him; a baby who rolls on his own may stay that way, but he is still always put down on his back
check.why: Once a baby can roll both ways on his own, he may sleep as he ends up. The caregiver still places him on his back every time and never props him with anything.

lessons.title: Childproofing Room by Room
lessons.mainIdea: Get down to a toddler's eye level and remove or lock what can burn, poison, shock, drown, cut or crush; the home does the supervising you cannot do every second.
reading: Get down on your hands and knees in the kitchen and look around. That is the view of a crawling baby, and from here the house is a different place: outlet slots at eye level, a dangling cord that leads to a hot iron, a cabinet with the dishwasher pods that look like candy, a trash can full of chicken skin, a pot handle sticking out over the edge of the stove. *Childproofing* is fixing the house from this view, before the child gets there, because no adult can watch a toddler every second and the house has to do part of the job.

Kitchen: cabinet latches on anything with cleaners, sharp tools or breakables; pot handles turned inward on the stove; the back burners first; no tablecloths a toddler can pull; hot drinks nowhere near the edge of a table. Bathroom: the water heater set at 120 °F or lower, because water at 140 °F can cause a serious burn in seconds; a toilet lock, since a toddler can drown in a few inches of water; medicines and vitamins in a locked cabinet up high, never in a purse on the floor. Never leave a child under about 5 alone in a bath, even for a moment, even to answer the door.

Everywhere: plastic covers or sliding plates on every outlet; cords for blinds cut short or cordless blinds, because looped cords strangle; furniture and televisions anchored to the wall, because a climbing toddler can pull a dresser over onto herself; gates at the top and bottom of stairs, with the top one screwed into the wall, not pressure-mounted; window guards or stops on upper-floor windows, since a screen does not hold a child; button batteries and magnets locked away, because swallowed ones burn through the gut. Small objects, coins, beads, balloons, anything that fits through a toilet-paper tube, out of reach of anyone under 3.

Poison: put *Poison Control*, 1-800-222-1222, in your phone and on the fridge. If a child swallows something, call before doing anything else, with the container in your hand; do not make the child vomit unless they tell you to. Keep a working smoke alarm on every level and a carbon monoxide alarm near sleeping areas, and test them monthly. Then, after all of this, still watch. Childproofing buys the seconds between when a toddler starts something and when an adult gets there. It does not replace the adult.

words.d: changing a home so that what a child can reach cannot burn, poison, shock, drown, cut or crush her
the free national hotline, 1-800-222-1222, to call first when a child may have swallowed something harmful
fastening furniture and televisions to the wall so a climbing child cannot tip them over
a burn from hot liquid or steam; a home water heater at 120 °F or lower helps prevent it

look.title: Childproofing Figures Worth Knowing
rows: water temperature that burns skin in seconds
age below which small objects are a choking risk (years)
smoke and CO alarm test interval (months)
look.cite: Standard safety guidance from U.S. pediatric and consumer-safety sources; Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222
look.prompt: A landlord says the water heater is set at 140 °F "so the dishes get clean." Using the table, explain what a toddler in that apartment could suffer and what the setting should be.

check.q: What is the recommended maximum setting for a home water heater where children live?
check.why: At 120 °F or lower, tap water is far less likely to scald a child. Water at 140 °F can cause a serious burn in seconds.

check.q: A two-year-old is found with an open bottle of children's vitamins and several missing. What is the first action?
choices: Make her vomit right away
Call Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, with the bottle in hand and follow their instructions
Give her a large glass of milk to dilute it
Wait to see whether she gets sick
check.why: Poison Control is called first, before anything else. Never induce vomiting unless they say to; some substances cause more harm coming back up.

check.q: Why should a stair gate at the top of the stairs be screwed into the wall rather than pressure-mounted?
choices: Pressure gates are more expensive
Screwed gates are easier for adults to open
A pressure gate can give way when a child pushes or leans on it, and at the top of stairs that means a fall
Pressure gates are only for doorways in rented homes
check.why: A pressure-mounted gate holds by friction and can be pushed loose. At the top of a staircase, that failure means a fall down the stairs.

lessons.title: Car Seats by Stage
lessons.mainIdea: A child rides rear-facing as long as the seat allows, then forward-facing with a harness, then in a booster until the seat belt fits, and always in the back seat until at least 13.
reading: A car crash is the leading way children in the United States die from injury, and most of those deaths involve a child who was unrestrained or in the wrong seat. The right seat depends on the child's size and stage, not just age, and the stages go in a fixed order. Every stage has one job: to keep the child's body from moving forward into the crash, and to spread the force across the strongest parts of the body, the back, shoulders and hips, instead of the neck and belly.

Stage one is *rear-facing*. Infants and toddlers ride facing the back of the car, in an infant seat or a convertible seat, for as long as the seat allows, until they reach its top height or weight limit. Most children can stay rear-facing well past age 2. The reason is the neck: a young child's head is heavy and the neck is weak, and in a frontal crash a rear-facing seat cradles the head, neck and spine together. Legs bent against the seat back are fine. Stage two is *forward-facing* with a five-point harness, again until the child outgrows the seat's limits; the top tether strap must be attached to the anchor in the car so the seat cannot pitch forward.

Stage three is the *booster seat*, which lifts the child so the adult lap-and-shoulder belt fits: the lap belt low across the thighs, not the belly, and the shoulder belt across the middle of the shoulder and chest, not the neck or under the arm. A child stays in a booster until the belt fits without it, which for most children is somewhere around 4 feet 9 inches tall and between about 8 and 12 years old. Stage four is the seat belt alone, in the back seat until at least age 13, because the front airbag is built for an adult body.

Installation is where most seats fail. A correctly installed seat moves less than an inch side to side or front to back at the belt path. The harness is snug enough that you cannot pinch a fold of strap at the collarbone, with the chest clip at armpit level. No puffy coats under the harness, because they compress in a crash and leave the straps loose; put the coat on backward over the buckled harness instead. Seats expire, usually six to ten years after manufacture, and any seat that has been in a crash is replaced. Many fire departments and hospitals have certified technicians who will check an installation for free.

words.d: the first car-seat stage, facing the back of the car, kept as long as the seat's height and weight limits allow
the second stage, a seat with a five-point harness and a top tether, until the child outgrows its limits
the third stage, which raises the child so the adult lap-and-shoulder belt fits correctly
the strap from the top of a forward-facing seat to an anchor in the car that keeps the seat from pitching forward

look.title: Four Kids, One Minivan
look.text: A family is loading a minivan. Baby Sofia, 11 months and 22 pounds, is placed forward-facing so she can see her siblings. Leo, 3, is in a forward-facing harness seat, but the top tether is dangling loose behind it. Maya, 6 and 45 inches tall, is in the back with just a seat belt; the shoulder belt crosses her neck so she has tucked it behind her. Jordan, 12, calls shotgun and climbs into the front passenger seat. It is 20 °F out and everyone is wearing a puffy coat.
look.prompt: Find every error, put each child in the right stage, and explain what would happen to each child's body in a frontal crash with the seating as described.

check.q: A 20-month-old has not yet reached the height or weight limit of her convertible seat. Which direction should she face?
choices: Forward-facing, because she is over one year old
Rear-facing, as long as the seat's limits allow
Whichever direction she prefers
Forward-facing, because rear-facing bends her legs
check.why: Children ride rear-facing until they outgrow the seat's limits, usually well past age 2. Bent legs are fine; a protected neck is the point.

check.q: In a booster seat, where should the lap belt and shoulder belt sit?
choices: Lap belt across the belly, shoulder belt across the neck
Lap belt across the thighs, shoulder belt under the arm
Lap belt low across the thighs, shoulder belt across the middle of the shoulder and chest
Both belts tucked behind the child so they do not rub
check.why: The belt must load the hips and shoulder. A belt on the belly or neck injures soft tissue in a crash, and a belt behind the back does nothing.

check.q: Why should a child not wear a puffy winter coat under a car-seat harness?
choices: The coat makes the child too warm
The coat blocks the chest clip from closing
The coat scratches the harness straps
The padding compresses in a crash, leaving the harness loose enough for the child to move
check.why: A harness that seems snug over a puffy coat is loose once the coat flattens. Buckle the harness over thin clothes and put the coat on backward over it.

lessons.title: Choking: Prevent It, Then Act
lessons.mainIdea: Cut round foods, keep small objects away from children under 3, and know the back blows and thrusts for a choking child who cannot breathe or cough.
reading: A grape is the perfect size and shape to plug a toddler's airway. So is a hot dog, cut into rounds, and a cherry tomato, and a hard candy, and a chunk of raw carrot, and a marshmallow, and a spoonful of peanut butter, and popcorn. Children under about 4 have small airways and are still learning to chew and swallow in the right order, which is why food is the most common thing children choke on. The fix is mechanical: cut grapes and cherry tomatoes in quarters lengthwise, hot dogs in long thin strips, cook carrots soft, and skip nuts, hard candy, popcorn and whole marshmallows for anyone under 4.

Objects: anything that fits through a toilet-paper tube is a *choking hazard* for a child under 3. Coins, buttons, marbles, beads, small toy parts, the eyes on a stuffed animal, the cap of a pen. Latex balloons, whole or in pieces, are the leading non-food cause of choking death in children; a torn balloon molds to the throat. Check the age label on toys, keep an older sibling's small toys in a separate bin up high, and get down on the floor and look. Meals happen sitting down, at the table, with an adult watching: no eating while walking, running, laughing hard or riding in the car.

Know the difference between a child who is coughing and a child who is *choking*. A child who is coughing, crying or talking is moving air; stay close, stay calm and let the cough do its work. A child who cannot cough, cannot cry, cannot speak, is turning blue or is making a high-pitched sound with a look of panic has a blocked airway, and the seconds count. For a child over 1 who is conscious: five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand, then five *abdominal thrusts*, fist just above the navel, pulling in and up, and repeat until the object comes out or the child goes limp. For an infant under 1: lay her face down along your forearm, head lower than body, five back blows, turn her over, five chest thrusts with two fingers on the breastbone, repeat.

Call 911, or have someone else call, as soon as you know the airway is blocked. If the child goes limp, begin CPR, and never sweep a finger blindly into the mouth; you can push the object deeper. This lesson describes the steps. It does not replace a class. A Red Cross or American Heart Association course in infant and child CPR takes an afternoon, includes practice on a manikin, and is the single most useful thing a babysitter or new parent can do before the first night alone with a child.

words.d: any food or object small or round enough to block a young child's airway; for objects, anything that fits through a toilet-paper tube
quick inward and upward pushes with a fist just above the navel, used to clear a blocked airway in a conscious child over 1
five firm strikes between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand, the first step for a choking child or infant
cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths for a person who is not breathing; learn it in a certified class

look.title: Sort the Snack Tray
look.text: A tray for a playdate of two-year-olds holds: whole grapes, cheese cubes, cherry tomatoes, banana slices, popcorn, hot dog rounds, cooked soft peas, whole almonds, mini marshmallows, and strawberry halves. A bowl of small round balloons for a game sits on the same table. The kids will eat while running between the living room and the yard.
look.prompt: Rewrite the tray: which foods stay as they are, which are fixed and how (be exact about the cut), which come off entirely? Then fix the two things about the setting that are not about the food.

check.q: How should grapes be served to a two-year-old?
choices: Cut in quarters lengthwise
Whole, since they are soft
Cut in half crosswise into two rounds
Peeled but whole
check.why: A whole or round-sliced grape is the size and shape of a toddler's airway. Quartered lengthwise, the pieces are thin and cannot plug it.

check.q: A three-year-old at dinner suddenly starts coughing hard and loudly, eyes watering. What is the right first response?
choices: Start abdominal thrusts immediately
Stay close, stay calm and let her keep coughing, since a loud cough means air is moving
Sweep her mouth with a finger to find the food
Give her a drink of water to wash it down
check.why: A child who can cough loudly has a partly open airway and the cough is the best tool. Thrusts, finger sweeps and liquids can make it worse.

check.q: An eight-month-old is choking on a button and cannot cry or make sound. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Abdominal thrusts, then finger sweep
Hold her upside down by the ankles and shake
Five back blows face down along the forearm, then five chest thrusts with two fingers, repeat, with 911 called
Wait to see if she coughs it out on her own
check.why: For an infant under 1, the sequence is back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts. A silent infant has a blocked airway and 911 is called at once.

lessons.title: Before the Parents Leave
lessons.mainIdea: The information a sitter gathers in the first ten minutes, numbers, allergies, routines and rules, is what makes the next four hours safe.
reading: The parents have their coats on and the car is running. This is the moment to slow down, because everything you do not ask now you will have to guess later. A good sitter arrives ten to fifteen minutes early with a list, and a good family has the list already on the fridge. Either way the first section is *emergency information*: both parents' cell numbers, where they will be, a second adult to call if the parents cannot be reached, the pediatrician's number, Poison Control, and the house address with the nearest cross street, written down, because in a real emergency your mind goes blank.

The second section is the children. Names and ages. *Allergies*, with the exact reaction and the exact treatment: where the epinephrine auto-injector is and a demonstration of how to use it, where the inhaler is, what foods are off limits. The nine major food allergens the law requires on every label are milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame; if a child is allergic to one, you read every label before serving anything. Medications: what, how much, when, and never anything not on the list. Medical conditions. Fears, comfort objects, the word the toddler uses for the bathroom.

The third section is the plan. What and when they eat. Bedtime, in steps, including what happens when the four-year-old asks for the third book. Where each child sleeps and the safe-sleep rules for the baby. What is allowed: which shows, how much screen time, whether they may go outside, which rooms are off limits. House rules for you: whether you may have a friend over (the usual answer is no), whether you may use the stove, what to do if someone comes to the door (do not open it), and how to lock up. Ask where the flashlight, the first-aid kit and the fire extinguisher are.

Then do a walk-through while the parents are still there. Look at the crib. Look at the stove, the door locks, the stairs. Ask what you are unsure about now; a question at 6:00 p.m. is free and the same question at 9:30 p.m. is a phone call to a parent at dinner. Finally, agree on when they will be home and how you will get home. When they return, report: what the children ate, when they slept, anything unusual, in order. Parents trust the sitter who tells them about the small cough more than the one who says "everything was fine."

words.d: the numbers and facts a sitter needs before anything goes wrong: parents, backup adult, doctor, Poison Control, the home address
a device such as an EpiPen that injects epinephrine into the outer thigh to treat a severe allergic reaction; call 911 after using it
milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame, which U.S. law requires to be named on food labels
a quick tour of the home with the parents to locate exits, hazards, the crib, the first-aid kit and the extinguisher

look.title: Ten Minutes at the Door
look.text: A parent hands you a sticky note: "Back by 11. Kids ate. Bed at 8. Thanks!" and reaches for the doorknob. There are two children, about 2 and 6. You have never been in this house. You know the parent's first name and nothing else.
look.prompt: Write the eight questions you ask before the door closes, in the order you would ask them, and say which one you would refuse to let them leave without answering.

check.q: Why should a sitter have the house address written down, even though she is standing in the house?
choices: Because parents often forget to tell sitters the address
Because a 911 dispatcher will not send help without a cross street
Because it is required on the sitter's tax forms
Because in an emergency people forget details, and 911 needs the address immediately
check.why: Stress wipes out memory. Written emergency information is read aloud, not recalled, and the address is the first thing 911 needs.

check.q: A parent says their five-year-old is allergic to peanuts and hands you an epinephrine auto-injector. What else must you ask before they leave?
choices: What the reaction looks like and how to use the injector, with a demonstration
Whether the child likes peanuts
Which brand of peanut butter to avoid
Whether the allergy will go away
check.why: A sitter must recognize the reaction and be able to use the injector. Seeing it demonstrated is the only way to be ready.

check.q: Which of these is a food allergen that U.S. law requires to be named on food labels?
choices: Corn
Sesame
Strawberries
Tomatoes
check.why: The nine major allergens are milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added to the list in 2023.

lessons.title: Activities by Age
lessons.mainIdea: A good sitter matches the activity to the child's stage, keeps it simple, and puts the phone away.
reading: A sitter who arrives with only a phone has a long evening ahead. A sitter who arrives with a plan for the age has an easy one. The plan does not have to be elaborate. It has to fit the stage, be safe for the space, and be something the sitter is genuinely willing to do on the floor. The first rule of every activity is *active supervision*: the sitter is in the room, watching and within reach, not in the next room checking messages. Most childhood injuries happen in the minute an adult looked away.

Infants, birth to 1: talk, sing, make faces, hold them where they can see you, shake a rattle, read a board book, lie on the floor for tummy time while they are awake and watched. Keep it slow; an overstimulated baby cries. Toddlers, 1 to 3: stacking cups, big blocks, push toys, a cardboard box, fat crayons on big paper, a bin of water on a towel with cups to pour (never unwatched), a song with hand motions, a walk to look at trucks. Expect short attention, about five minutes per activity, and expect to repeat the same thing many times.

Preschoolers, 3 to 5: pretend play with you in a role, a couch-cushion fort, play dough, simple board games with turns, drawing together, a scavenger hunt for five things that are blue, reading the same book with voices, helping make a snack. They love jobs: setting the table, sorting socks. School-age, 6 and up: card games, real board games, building projects, cooking something simple together if the parents allow the stove, a walk or ball game outside if allowed, and honestly just talking. Older kids often test a sitter with "my mom lets me." The answer is friendly and fixed: "I'll check with her next time. Tonight the rule is what she told me."

Screens are a tool, not a plan. If the parents allow a show, use it for the twenty minutes you need to put the baby down, then turn it off. Have a quiet wind-down before bed: lights lower, voices lower, a bath if planned, books. Keep the space picked up as you go so the house the parents come home to is the house they left. And if a child is upset for you in a way you cannot fix, or sick, or something feels wrong, call the parents. That is not failure. That is the job.

words.d: watching children closely, within reach, with attention on them rather than on a phone
matched to what a child at that stage can do safely and enjoy
the quiet period before bed with lower lights, lower voices and calm activities

look.title: Plan the Evening
look.text: You are sitting from 5:30 to 9:30 for a 9-month-old, a 3-year-old and a 7-year-old. Dinner is ready to heat. The baby's bottle is at 6:30 and bed at 7; the 3-year-old's bed is at 7:45; the 7-year-old's is at 8:30. The parents allow one 25-minute show. The house has a yard, a bin of blocks, crayons, a deck of cards and three picture books.
look.prompt: Write a schedule for the four hours, with one activity per age for each block of time, showing where the show goes and how you keep the two older children busy while you put the baby down.

check.q: Which activity fits a two-year-old best?
choices: A 100-piece jigsaw puzzle
A card game with rules
Stacking cups and pouring water from cup to cup in a bin, with the sitter beside her
A half-hour of drawing detailed pictures
check.why: Toddlers have short attention and learn through simple repeated actions. Water play, watched closely, is ideal; puzzles and card games are for older children.

check.q: A nine-year-old says, "My dad lets me stay up until eleven on Fridays," but the list says 8:30. What is the best reply?
choices: "Okay, if he lets you."
"You're lying, and I'm telling him."
"Let's compromise on ten."
"I'll ask him next time. Tonight the rule is what he told me: 8:30."
check.why: The parents' written instructions are the rule for the sitter. A friendly, fixed answer avoids both an argument and an unauthorized change.

check.q: When is the best time to use the one show the parents allowed?
choices: While the sitter puts the baby to bed, so the older children are occupied and safe
At the very beginning, to break the ice
Right at bedtime, so the child falls asleep to it
Whenever the child asks for it
check.why: A show is a tool for the minutes when the sitter must give full attention to one child. It is not a wind-down and not on demand.

lessons.title: Recognizing and Reporting Abuse
lessons.mainIdea: Anyone who cares for children learns the signs of abuse and neglect and knows that reporting a reasonable concern is the way a child gets help.
reading: This lesson is hard, and it belongs here, because the people most likely to notice that a child is being hurt are the people who see the child every day: teachers, child care workers, coaches, babysitters, neighbors, the older cousin. *Child abuse* is harm done to a child by an adult or older child: physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, and *neglect*, the failure to provide food, shelter, clothing, medical care or supervision a child needs. Neglect is the most common form. Most abuse is done by someone the child knows and trusts, not a stranger.

Signs are patterns, not single events. Every child gets bruises on shins and knees; bruises on the back, the belly, the face, the ears, or in the shape of a hand or an object, or on a baby who cannot yet move on her own, are different. Burns in a pattern, like a cigarette or a hot object. Injuries the child explains in a way that does not fit, or that change with each telling. A child who flinches when an adult moves quickly, who is afraid to go home, who is hungry all the time, who comes to school in the same dirty clothes in winter, who is left alone at an age when he cannot be. Sexual knowledge or behavior far beyond the child's age. A sudden change: a cheerful child who goes silent, a child who starts wetting the bed again, a teenager who stops eating.

If a child tells you something, stay calm, listen, and believe her. Do not interrogate; do not promise to keep it secret; do not react with horror, because she will stop talking. Say: "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault. I'm going to get help." Then write down exactly what she said, in her words, with the date. In Illinois, teachers, child care workers, medical staff, coaches and many others are *mandated reporters*: the law requires them to report a reasonable suspicion of abuse or neglect. Anyone can report. The Illinois DCFS child abuse hotline is 1-800-25-ABUSE (1-800-252-2873), and a child in immediate danger is a 911 call.

You do not need proof. You do not investigate. You report what you saw and heard, and trained people decide what comes next. Reporting in good faith is protected by law; not reporting, for a mandated reporter, is not. The fear that stops most people, what if I am wrong, has an answer: if you are wrong, a caseworker makes a visit and nothing happens. If you are right and you said nothing, a child stays where she is. This chapter began with a list on a refrigerator. A child's safety is a longer list, and the last line on it is: when you see something, say something to the people whose job it is to help.

words.d: physical, sexual or emotional harm done to a child by an adult or older child
failing to provide the food, shelter, clothing, medical care or supervision a child needs; the most common form of maltreatment
a person, such as a teacher or child care worker, whom the law requires to report reasonable suspicion of abuse or neglect
the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services line for reporting suspected abuse or neglect: 1-800-25-ABUSE (1-800-252-2873)

look.title: What a Sitter Noticed
look.text: Over three months of Saturday sitting, a sitter notices: the six-year-old has had bruises on his upper arms twice, in a row of small ovals; he says he "fell." He asks for seconds and thirds at every meal and hides crackers in his pockets. Tonight he asked whether she could stay and not go home. His four-year-old sister seems fine. The sitter likes the parents and does not want to cause trouble.
look.prompt: List the signs, decide whether this is a reasonable concern, and write exactly what the sitter should do next, in order. What should she not do?

check.q: A five-year-old tells her babysitter that a relative touches her in a way she does not like, and asks her to promise not to tell. What is the right response?
choices: Promise, so she keeps trusting you, and then decide later
Ask detailed questions to find out exactly what happened before telling anyone
Stay calm, thank her, tell her it is not her fault, explain that you have to get help, and report it
Tell her she must be mistaken and change the subject
check.why: A child who discloses needs calm belief and a clear promise of help, not secrecy. The sitter reports; trained people investigate.

check.q: Which of these bruise patterns is most likely a sign of abuse rather than ordinary play?
choices: Bruises on the shins of a seven-year-old
A scraped knee on a four-year-old who fell off a bike
A bump on the forehead of a toddler learning to walk
Bruises on the back and upper arms in the shape of fingers on a six-year-old
check.why: Play bruises land on shins, knees and foreheads. Bruises on the back, belly or upper arms, especially in the shape of a hand, are a warning sign.

check.q: What does a person need before reporting suspected child abuse to the Illinois DCFS hotline?
choices: A reasonable suspicion based on what they saw or heard; proof is not required
Photographs of the injuries
Permission from the parents
A signed statement from the child
check.why: Reporters do not investigate. A reasonable concern, reported in good faith, is enough and is protected by law; DCFS decides what happens next.

review.q: A two-year-old bites another child at day care. Which response is guidance rather than punishment?
choices: Bite him back so he learns how it feels
A firm "Biting hurts. Teeth are for food," then redirect him to a teething toy and comfort the other child
A twenty-minute time-out in the hallway
Taking away his favorite blanket for the day
review.why: Guidance states the limit, replaces the behavior and stays calm. Biting back is abuse, and long or unrelated consequences teach a two-year-old nothing.

review.q: Which is the complete safe-sleep rule for an infant?
choices: On the back, with a light blanket, in the parents' bed
On the stomach, on a firm mattress, alone
On the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the crib with nothing else in it
On the side, with bumper pads, in a bassinet
review.why: Back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing else in the sleep space, and room-sharing without bed-sharing.

review.q: A landlord sets the water heater to 150 °F. Why does this matter for a family with a toddler?
choices: Higher temperatures are fine because toddlers are not bathed in tap water
It only matters for the dishwasher
It saves money on energy bills
Water above 120 °F can scald a child in seconds; 120 °F or lower is the recommended maximum
review.why: A home water heater should be set at 120 °F or lower. Water at 140 °F or more burns skin in seconds.

review.q: A three-year-old, 35 pounds, has outgrown the height limit of her rear-facing seat. What is the next stage?
choices: A forward-facing seat with a five-point harness and the top tether attached
A booster seat with the adult belt
The adult seat belt alone in the back seat
The front passenger seat with the airbag off
review.why: After rear-facing comes a forward-facing harness seat, kept until she outgrows its limits. Boosters come later, and the front seat waits until 13.

review.q: A four-year-old is eating and suddenly cannot cough, cannot speak and is turning blue. What is the correct first action?
choices: Give her water
Five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts, repeat, and call 911
Sweep her mouth with a finger
Lay her down and start chest compressions
review.why: A silent child with a blocked airway needs back blows and abdominal thrusts at once. Finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

review.q: Which item on a babysitter's information sheet is the one to call first if a toddler swallows a cleaning product?
choices: The pediatrician's office
The parents' cell number
Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
The backup neighbor
review.why: Poison Control gives immediate instructions for the specific product. Parents are called right after.

review.q: A sitter for a two-year-old lays out whole grapes, cheese cubes and hot dog rounds. What is the safe fix?
choices: Serve them all; two-year-olds can chew
Serve only the cheese; grapes and hot dogs are not allowed under 4
Cut the grapes in half
Quarter the grapes lengthwise, cut the hot dog into thin strips, and serve at the table while watching
review.why: Round foods the size of an airway are cut into thin lengthwise pieces. Meals are eaten sitting, with an adult watching.

review.q: A teacher notices a seven-year-old who flinches when adults move quickly, has bruises on his back and says his stepfather "gets mad." What must the teacher do?
choices: Report the concern to the Illinois DCFS hotline; teachers are mandated reporters and proof is not required
Wait until she has photographs and a second incident
Ask the stepfather about it at pickup
Tell the child to let her know if it happens again
review.why: Mandated reporters are required by law to report reasonable suspicion. Investigating or confronting the family is not the teacher's job and can put the child at greater risk.
